Kandariya Mahadeva Temple, Khajuraho, in 3D

The Kandariya Mahadeva is the largest standing temple at Khajuraho, built during the Chandela dynasty, who ruled the region in the 10th and 11th centuries CE. This model is built from the measurements Alexander Cunningham published from his 1864–65 survey and from his ground plan. Drag to turn it, pinch or scroll to zoom, and switch the roofs off to see the plan and the sanctum.

What is measured and what is estimated

LengthMeasured33.2 m (109 ft) externally
WidthMeasuredAbout 18.1 m (59½ ft) externally; Fergusson gives 60 ft (18.3 m)
HeightMeasured35.5 m (116½ ft) above the ground; 26.8 m (88 ft) above its own floor
Floor levelMeasured8.7 m (28½ ft) above the ground: the difference between the two heights
PlanDocumentedPortico, hall (mandapa), great hall with transepts (maha-mandapa), vestibule (antarala) and sanctum (garbha-griha), with a passage round the sanctum lit by three open porticoes at the back and sides: a "double cross"
RoofsDocumentedEach part has its own roof, rising in steps from the low pyramid over the entrance to the tall spire over the sanctum
SanctumDocumentedA marble liṅga, shown here as a plain labelled shape
SculptureDocumentedCunningham counted 226 statues inside and 646 outside, 872 in all (not modelled)
DynastyDocumentedBuilt during the Chandela dynasty, who ruled the region in the 10th and 11th centuries CE
Chamber sizes, wall and roof heightsEstimatedRead from the published plan and photographs, not from a measured section
Smaller spires round the towerEstimatedTheir number and grouping are not taken from a measured drawing
Terrace and base mouldingsEstimatedHow the 8.7 m rise divides between the shared terrace and the temple's own base
PersonIllustrative1.7 m (5 ft 7 in), for scale

About this model

Cunningham describes the temple as having the usual portico, hall, great hall, vestibule and sanctum, "each of which has its separate pinnacled roof rising in regular gradation from the low pyramid of the entrance to the lofty spire of the sanctum". A second pair of transepts lights the passage round the sanctum, which is why he calls the plan a large double cross rather than a single one.

What the model does not show: the sculpture. Cunningham counted 872 statues on and in the temple, and no deity figures are modelled here. The sanctum holds a marble liṅga, drawn as a plain shape with a label.
